articles.author: David Miller
articles.description:
Leave Content-Type unset in the request options when fetch() sends FormData. The browser adds the multipart boundary needed by that body.
Build the form with const data = new FormData(); data.append("image", file); and pass it as the request body. A manually supplied Content-Type: multipart/form-data omits the boundary that the browser normally adds. Apply this rule to requests whose body is FormData.
Check a shared request helper for an unconditional JSON or multipart header before blaming the image bytes. Keep any authorization headers your application actually requires. Inspect the request and the server's response using a small non-sensitive test image.
The MDN FormData guide explains the boundary requirement. In a bug report, identify the body type and header construction without copying credentials into the report.
I work on Morphio, our image project at https://morphio.online/. These notes describe image preparation and review; they do not require a particular editing tool.
articles.title: Let the browser set the multipart boundary for an image upload

ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Them
When an ACH transfer fails, you don't get a generic "payment declined" message. Instead, the National Automated Clearing House Association (Nacha) returns a specific code—one of 85 standardized reasons why the transaction bounced. As a developer building payment systems, understanding these codes isn't optional; it's the foundation of reliable payout logic.
ACH is the backbone of direct deposit, bill pay, and B2B transfers in the US. Unlike card networks that settle in seconds, ACH batches process in windows (typically overnight), and returns can arrive 1–5 business days later. When a return lands, your system must:
Identify the failure reason
Decide whether to retry, escalate, or switch payment rails
Update the payout record an…

articles.description:
Environment: CODESYS V3.5 SP22 | Target: CODESYS Control Win V3 x64 simulation
The previous lesson built a minimal host/controller loop: three axes that were hand-rolled — FB_SimAxis parsed commands and climbed position itself. The motion was real; the axes were fake.
This lesson meets a real axis.
Start from motion control. In short: an axis is the motion counterpart of a control object — setpoints and status on one side, drive + motor + encoder on the other, bound by mapping.

Motion control FBs share a common timing shape: execute edge, busy, done, error.

Drives speak a state machine: Not ready to switch on → Switch on disabled → Ready to switch on → Switched on → Operation enabled.


Motion API (MC_*)
Axis object (state + setpoints)
Drive profile (CiA 402 / fieldbus)
Names stay fixed; the implementation can be simulated or real.

Logical axis vs physical axis
Mapping binds them
MC timing is consistent across FBs
CiA 402 is the drive language
Same program can run on sim or hardware
articles.title: CODESYS Applied Practice — Axes (Part 1)
